# Results -- Study 273 (Lego-Returns) on the S&P 500 price tape

*Generated by [`examples/verify.py`](../examples/verify.py). The LEGO secondary-market
index (annual levels, base 100 at 1986) is hardcoded in [`data.py`](../lego_returns/data.py),
curated from Dobrynskaya & Kishilova (2022) and extended to 2024. S&P 500 calendar-year
PRICE returns are from `_cache/^GSPC_split_only.parquet` (split-adjusted, no dividends).
Match the fingerprint below to confirm you hold the same data. As-of **2026-06-17**.*

## Data stamp

| Source | Window | n | Fingerprint |
|---|---|---|---|
| S&P 500 (price-only, Dec/Dec, split-adjusted) | 1987-2024 | 38 years | `c2f1ae5a05d5` |
| LEGO secondary-market index | 1986-2024 (levels) | 38 returns | hardcoded constant |

## Headline returns (price-only, gross unless noted)

| Leg | CAGR 1987-2024 |
|---|--:|
| LEGO index (gross) | **8.30%** |
| LEGO index (net, 12% one-way fee over 5-yr hold) | **5.90%** |
| S&P 500 (price-only) | **8.76%** |
| S&P 500 (+ ~2%/yr dividends, total return) | ~10.76% |

The gross LEGO basket already *trails* the price-only S&P (8.30% vs 8.76%), before
charging any cost of selling and before crediting the equity holder's dividends.

## The decisive test -- annual excess return (LEGO minus S&P)

| Measure | Gross | Net (12% fee / 5-yr hold) |
|---|--:|--:|
| Mean annual excess return | **-1.83 pp/yr** | **-4.23 pp/yr** |
| Newey-West HAC t-stat | **-0.668** | **-1.544** |

The mean excess is **negative** and statistically indistinguishable from zero
(gross), or negative-and-approaching-significant against LEGO (net). The bar for a
REAL signal -- a **positive** mean excess with HAC |t| >= 2 -- is not met in either
direction of the claim. Annual excess returns have negligible autocorrelation, so
the HAC lag is ~1 and the HAC t is close to the plain t.

## Diversification claim (CAPM, the one true half)

| Metric | Value |
|---|--:|
| Beta of LEGO on S&P | **0.011** |
| Alpha | +8.22%/yr |
| Correlation | **0.067** |

LEGO genuinely does **not** co-move with equities (beta ~0.01, correlation ~0.07).
This is the real part of the Dobrynskaya-Kishilova finding. But a near-zero-beta
asset whose *level* of return trails the market is a diluting hedge, not alpha.

## Paired sign test

LEGO beat the S&P in **16 of 38 years (42.1%)** -- below a coin flip.
Binomial p (vs 50%, greater) = **0.872**: no evidence LEGO wins more often than not.

## Cost sensitivity

Net LEGO CAGR (%) by one-way fee x holding years (real tape):

| fee \\ hold | 3 yr | 5 yr | 10 yr |
|---|--:|--:|--:|
| 0% | 8.30 | 8.30 | 8.30 |
| 6% | ~6.3 | ~7.1 | ~7.7 |
| 12% | ~4.3 | 5.90 | ~7.1 |
| 15% | ~3.3 | ~5.3 | ~6.8 |

Only the fee-free / very-long-hold corner even ties the price-only S&P (8.76%);
under any realistic fee assumption LEGO trails, and it trails the total-return S&P
(~10.8%) everywhere.

## Survivorship / selection caveat

The hardcoded index is built (like all published collectible indices) from sets
that kept trading and were tracked. Flops, liquidations and sets that left the
resale market are under-represented, biasing the index **upward**. The true
realisable LEGO return for a typical buyer (paying RRP, storing for years, paying
marketplace fees) is **below** the numbers above. This bias is named on the Signal
axis.

## Verdict

- **Signal -- NONE.** Mean annual excess return is negative; Newey-West HAC
  t = -0.67 (gross), -1.54 (net). No positive equity-beating premium, let alone a
  robust t >= 2. The index is survivorship-/selection-biased upward, so even the
  flat gross result is generous. The diversification half of the claim (beta ~0.01)
  is real, but low beta is not a return signal.
- **Tradability -- MIRAGE.** Net of a one-way ~12% resale fee, storage,
  insurance, single-item illiquidity and selection risk, the LEGO CAGR (~5.9%)
  trails a one-click, dividend-paying, ~0.03%-fee index fund. There is no scalable
  way to capture even the paper return.
- **Busted (as an investment).** LEGO is a fun, nostalgic, genuinely low-correlation
  collectible. The "retired sets beat the stock market" headline does not survive
  the price-only benchmark, dividends, resale fees, and survivorship bias.
